title: India's GCC Boom Hits a Talent Wall as AI Skills Gap Widens
excerpt: Global Capability Centers added nearly 200,000 jobs in India last year — twice the IT services sector — but a 38-42% shortage in AI and data talent threatens to slow the next phase of growth.
body:
• India's GCCs added nearly 200,000 net employees in FY2026, almost double the 110,000 by IT services firms, according to TeamLease Digital data
  • The country now hosts 2,117 GCCs employing 2.36 million professionals and generating $98.4 billion in revenue
  • A 38-42% supply gap exists in AI and data roles across India's GCC ecosystem, with demand for AI specialists up over 300% since 2024
  • Tier-2 cities like Coimbatore, Kochi and Ahmedabad are gaining traction as alternative hubs amid talent concentration in metros

India's Global Capability Centers have overtaken traditional IT services firms in hiring for the third straight year, but a widening shortage of AI and data talent is emerging as the biggest constraint on the sector's growth trajectory.

GCCs added nearly 200,000 net employees in fiscal 2026, almost twice the 110,000 added by IT services firms, according to TeamLease Digital data cited by The Economic Times. The numbers mark a structural shift: multinationals are increasingly moving AI, cloud and cybersecurity work inside their own captive centers rather than outsourcing it.

The Scale of India's GCC Ecosystem

India now hosts 2,117 active GCCs employing approximately 2.36 million professionals, according to a Nasscom and Zinnov report released in May. The ecosystem generated $98.4 billion in revenue in FY2026, and more than 1,200 GCCs had embedded AI and machine learning capabilities.

GCCs are no longer just cost-saving back-office operations. They handle AI platforms, cloud architecture, product engineering and cybersecurity — work where companies want tighter control over data and intellectual property. Deloitte's Rohan Lobo told The Economic Times that IP control, data protection and regulatory compliance are pushing more companies toward captive centers.

The Talent Crunch

The demand is outrunning supply. Quess Corp's Q4 FY26 findings estimated a 38% to 42% gap in AI and data skills across India's GCC ecosystem, according to TechRepublic. Demand for AI specialists has risen more than 300% since 2024, Lobo separately told The Economic Times.

"Supply gaps ranging from 18% to 43% across AI/ML Ops, platform engineering, cybersecurity and GenAI operations show the urgent need for faster upskilling and stronger talent mobility."

— Kapil Joshi, CEO, Quess IT Staffing

Mid-to-senior talent now accounts for more than 77% of GCC hiring, up from 60% in 2023, with demand strongest in AI, platform engineering, cloud, cybersecurity and data roles, according to IANS. The shift reflects GCCs moving from volume hiring to what Quess calls "precision over volume" — building deeper, more specialized capabilities rather than expanding headcount.

Beyond Bengaluru

While Bengaluru remains the primary hub — projected to lead Asia-Pacific office leasing with 12 million square feet expected in 2026, according to CBRE data cited by The Hindu Business Line — competition is intensifying. Hyderabad and Pune collectively account for 70% of India's 112 million square feet of GCC office absorption from 2020-2024.

Tier-2 cities are gaining ground. Coimbatore, Kochi and Ahmedabad are attracting GCC operations due to cost advantages and untapped talent pools. Bhartiya Converge CEO predicted India could host over 2,200 GCCs by 2030, employing 2.5-2.8 million people and surpassing $100 billion in value.

What's Next

For the Indian diaspora, the GCC boom represents both opportunity and competition. Return migration, cross-border hiring and the growing sophistication of India-based roles are reshaping career calculations for NRI professionals in AI, cloud and cybersecurity. Companies like Woodside Energy (Australia) and Airbus are opening new centers, adding to demand.

India's next phase of GCC growth depends less on demand — which remains robust — than on how quickly the country can train, hire and retain AI and cloud specialists. The gap between ambition and available talent will determine whether the sector hits its $100 billion target or stalls short of it.
